newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Rain, floods force 120,000 Filipinos to flee.
newsitem.headline: Rain, floods force 120,000 Filipinos to flee.

text.p: More than 120,000 Filipinos have fled their homes after the heaviest rains in a decade triggered massive flooding in the northern Philippines, killing 36 people, police and relief officials said on Tuesday.

President Fidel Ramos placed Manila and four provinces, which bore the brunt of three days of torrential rains, under a state of calamity. The administrative step allows the government to release emergency funds for rescue and rehabilitation. The weather bureau said it recorded 300 millimetres (12 inches) of rainfall in Manila during the 72-hour period that began on Saturday. The amount was equivalent to a whole month of rain -- unusual even for a country hit by an average of 20 typhoons a year.

"This is the worst...for the last 10 years," Prisco Nilo, chief of the bureau's forecasting section told Reuters. The rains brought Manila to a standstill on Monday, closing all its financial markets for the day.

Combined reports from the police and relief agencies put the death toll at 36, most of them drowning victims, as flood waters as deep as three metres (10 feet) submerged about half of Manila and about 300,000 homes in the city and provinces. Dozens were injured, police said.
The social welfare department said more than 120,000 people sought refuge in schoolhouses, government buildings and churches.
Manila's international airport remained without electricity for the second straight day after flood waters swamped the terminal building's basement and cut off its power supply.
Computers, baggage carousels and X-ray machines stopped working and scores of flights were delayed.
Immigration and customs officials had to work with portable lamps as more than 2,000 exasperated passengers jammed the terminal building waiting for their flights, a Reuter photographer said.
Many lay on the floor, some resting their heads on their luggage, as they fanned themselves with newspapers and cardboard to keep cool, he said.

"This is the first time in the history of the airport that this kind of disaster has happened," Elpidio Mendoza, assistant airport general manager, told Reuters. The rains that pounded the main island of Luzon, toppling power lines in Manila and surrounding cities and towns, were a boon to farmers, the Agriculture Department said. "The downpour was generally beneficial to rice and corn farmers to start land preparation, except for some tobacco and vegetable farmers whose crops were slightly affected," agriculture undersecretary Domingo Panganiban said in a report.
As the tropical depression that caused the torrents moved away from Luzon into the South China Sea, floods subsided around Manila and the affected provinces, clearing the way for relief operations.
